stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic knee osteoarthritis taking daily non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs presents with sudden-onset, severe generalised abdominal pain and board-like rigidity. An erect chest radiograph demonstrates a crescentic lucency beneath the right hemidiaphragm. What is the most likely underlying surgical cause of this radiological finding?
options: Acute uncomplicated gallstone biliary colic
Perforated peptic ulcer (duodenal or gastric)
Acute interstitial oedematous pancreatitis
Simple adhesive small bowel obstruction
Right-sided subpulmonic pleural effusion
optionRationales: Incorrect: Uncomplicated biliary colic causes episodic right upper quadrant pain without visceral perforation or free intraperitoneal gas.
Correct: Subdiaphragmatic free gas (pneumoperitoneum) on an erect chest radiograph is most commonly caused by a perforated duodenal or gastric ulcer, strongly linked to chronic NSAID use.
Incorrect: Acute pancreatitis typically causes epigastric pain radiating to the back and raised amylase, occasionally producing a sentinel loop rather than free subdiaphragmatic air.
Incorrect: Simple small bowel obstruction produces dilated loops and multiple air-fluid levels on abdominal X-ray, not free subphrenic gas unless complicated by perforation.
Incorrect: A subpulmonic pleural effusion causes apparent elevation of the hemidiaphragm above the lung base rather than a crescentic gas lucency beneath the diaphragm.
clinicalPearl: An erect chest X-ray is the most sensitive plain radiograph for detecting pneumoperitoneum (as little as 1–2 mL of free gas); perforated peptic ulcer is the commonest cause.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Crescentic lucency under the right hemidiaphragm represents pneumoperitoneum, classically caused by a perforated peptic ulcer.

sourceStation.title: Pneumoperitoneum (Right Subdiaphragmatic Air)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
03. Photograph of an erect chest X-ray (right-sided subdiaphragmatic air collection marked by arrow).
What is the abnormality shown by the arrow, and most possible cause?  [CXR omitted in text-only 2012 archive PDF]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Right-sided subdiaphragmatic air collection (pneumoperitoneum). Causes: Perforated duodenal/peptic ulcer (most common), Perforated diverticulum, Bowel malignancy perforation, Necrotising enterocolitis, Penetrating abdominal trauma, Subdiaphragmatic gas-forming abscess.

stem: A 66-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of severe colicky abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, progressive abdominal bloating, and failure to pass flatus or stool. Her plain abdominal radiograph is shown. After initial intravenous resuscitation and nasogastric decompression, which imaging modality is most definitive for confirming the transition point, identifying the underlying cause, and assessing for bowel ischaemia?
options: Oral barium follow-through meal study
Transabdominal pelvic ultrasonography alone
Flexible sigmoidoscopy without insufflation
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Tc-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy scan
optionRationales: Incorrect: Oral barium is contraindicated in suspected acute complete or strangulated bowel obstruction due to risks of inspissation and barium peritonitis if perforation occurs.
Incorrect: Abdominal ultrasound is limited by overlying bowel gas in acute obstruction and cannot reliably delineate deep transition points across the entire bowel.
Incorrect: Endoscopy carries perforation risk in acute obstruction and does not evaluate extraluminal causes such as adhesions or closed-loop small bowel ischaemia.

Correct: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the gold standard after initial plain radiography to confirm mechanical bowel obstruction, locate the transition point, determine the cause (e.g., adhesions, hernia, tumour), and detect strangulation.
Incorrect: Tc-99m pertechnetate scanning detects ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum rather than acute adult mechanical intestinal obstruction.
clinicalPearl: Plain erect and supine abdominal X-rays screen for dilated loops and air-fluid levels, whereas contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis defines the exact transition point, cause (adhesions, hernia, tumour, volvulus), and ischaemia.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Initial obstruction care includes NBM, IV fluids, and Ryle's tube decompression, followed by contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis to pinpoint the transition site and exclude strangulation.

sourceStation.title: Intestinal Obstruction
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
05. A 66-year-old female presents with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, bloating, and not passing gas or stool for 2 days.
What is the diagnosis? How do you investigate to confirm the diagnosis? Give 3 reasons for this happening.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Bowel (intestinal) obstruction. Investigations: Erect & supine Abdominal X-ray (dilated bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels), Contrast CT abdomen/pelvis (transition point & cause), Ultrasound / Endoscopy (once stabilised/selected). Causes: Strangulated hernia, Colorectal carcinoma, Adhesions, Volvulus (sigmoid/caecal), Faecal impaction, Ascaris lumbricoides bolus.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to the casualty unit with sudden epigastric pain and generalised abdominal guarding. An erect chest radiograph is obtained as shown. What is the principal radiological diagnosis?
options: Bilateral basal subpulmonic pleural effusions
Right-sided Chilaiditi colonic interposition
Bilateral subphrenic free air (pneumoperitoneum)
Bilateral apical tension pneumothoraces
Bilateral lower-lobe bullous emphysema
optionRationales: Incorrect: Subpulmonic effusions appear as homogeneous fluid opacity flattening and mimicking a high hemidiaphragm rather than sharp crescentic air lucencies beneath both domes.
Incorrect: Chilaiditi sign is asymptomatic colonic interposition beneath the right hemidiaphragm only, identifiable by visible colonic haustral markings rather than smooth bilateral free gas.

Correct: Smooth crescentic air lucencies beneath both the right and left hemidiaphragms (distinct from the gastric bubble below the left dome) confirm bilateral subphrenic pneumoperitoneum from hollow viscus perforation.
Incorrect: Pneumothorax demonstrates air within the pleural space outlining a retracted visceral pleural edge without peripheral lung markings, rather than subdiaphragmatic gas.
Incorrect: Bullous emphysema produces thin-walled parenchymal air spaces above the diaphragm within the lung fields rather than crescentic subphrenic collections.
clinicalPearl: Always check beneath both hemidiaphragms on an erect chest X-ray: free subphrenic gas appears as a crisp crescent outlining the diaphragm's inferior border, unlike haustrated bowel in Chilaiditi sign.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Gas under both hemidiaphragms indicates bilateral pneumoperitoneum from hollow viscus perforation and must be differentiated from hepatodiaphragmatic colonic interposition (Chilaiditi sign).

sourceStation.title: Bilateral Subphrenic Air Collection
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
01)
a) What is the radiological diagnosis?
b) Causes for that.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (a) Bilateral subphrenic air collection (pneumoperitoneum). (b) Causes: Perforated duodenal/peptic ulcer (most common), Ruptured appendix, Perforated diverticulum, Bowel obstruction with perforation, Bowel cancer, Penetrating trauma, Toxic megacolon.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with altered bowel habits, fresh per-rectal bleeding, and tenesmus. Colonoscopy demonstrates the ulcerated lesion shown at the rectosigmoid junction, and biopsy confirms the commonest malignant histological subtype. Which combination of imaging studies is specifically required next for complete local and distant staging prior to definitive surgical planning?
options: Contrast CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with pelvic MRI
Erect chest radiograph and supine abdominal radiograph alone
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and MRCP
Double-contrast barium enema and Meckel's radioisotope scan
Ultrasound KUB with technetium-99m bone scintigraphy
optionRationales: Correct: Colorectal adenocarcinoma (accounting for >95% of cases) requires contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis for nodal/liver/lung staging plus MRI pelvis to define local rectal/mesorectal fascia invasion.
Incorrect: Plain radiographs cannot stage hepatic metastases, regional lymphadenopathy, or circumferential resection margin involvement.
Incorrect: ERCP and MRCP evaluate the biliary tree and pancreatic duct rather than local or distant staging of rectosigmoid carcinoma.
Incorrect: Barium enema offers only luminal contour imaging without nodal or distant staging, and Meckel's scanning is irrelevant to colorectal neoplasia.
Incorrect: Ultrasound KUB and bone scans do not evaluate mesorectal tumour depth or pulmonary and hepatic parenchymal metastases adequately.
clinicalPearl: Colorectal adenocarcinoma staging combines CECT chest/abdomen/pelvis (distant liver/lung metastases) with pelvic MRI (local T-stage and mesorectal margin) plus baseline serum CEA for post-operative surveillance.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Preoperative staging of colorectal adenocarcinoma includes CECT chest/abdomen/pelvis and pelvic MRI alongside baseline CEA to guide surgery and post-operative recurrence monitoring.

sourceStation.title: Rectosigmoid Adenocarcinoma (Colonoscopy)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
01) 65-year-old male undergoing a colonoscopy shows the following appearance at the rectosigmoid junction.
1) List three (3) symptoms you will see in this patient.
2) What is the most probable histological diagnosis?
3) List two specific investigations that you should do to decide on further management.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Symptoms: Altered bowel habits (new-onset constipation/diarrhoea), Fresh per-rectal bleeding / blood mixed with stool, Tenesmus / feeling of incomplete evacuation, Unexplained weight loss / iron-deficiency anaemia. (2) Histology: Adenocarcinoma (colorectal adenocarcinoma). (3) Investigations: Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) chest, abdomen & pelvis (distant/nodal staging) and MRI pelvis (local rectal/mesorectal staging) ± serum CEA baseline and endoscopic biopsy.

stem: A 59-year-old man presents with acute peritonitis and hypotension; his erect chest radiograph is shown. Which pair of surgical pathologies represents the commonest non-traumatic causes of this radiological appearance?
options: Acute uncomplicated cholecystitis and ureteric colic
Adhesive small bowel obstruction and paralytic ileus
Acute oedematous pancreatitis and mesenteric adenitis
Intramural duodenal haematoma and splenic infarction
Perforated peptic ulcer and perforated colon carcinoma
optionRationales: Incorrect: Uncomplicated biliary and ureteric stone disease do not breach the gastrointestinal lumen to release free intraperitoneal air.
Incorrect: Simple mechanical obstruction or adynamic ileus distends intraluminal bowel gas without producing free subdiaphragmatic air unless perforation supervenes.
Incorrect: Acute oedematous pancreatitis and mesenteric adenitis cause retroperitoneal or peritoneal inflammation without hollow viscus perforation.
Incorrect: Intramural haematoma and splenic infarction remain confined to organ parenchyma or bowel wall without releasing intraluminal gas into the peritoneal cavity.

Correct: Free air under the diaphragm reflects gastrointestinal perforation, most frequently due to a perforated peptic (duodenal/gastric) ulcer or perforated colonic pathology (carcinoma, diverticulitis, or ruptured appendix).
clinicalPearl: Pneumoperitoneum in a patient with peritonism signals a surgical emergency—perforated peptic ulcer and colonic perforation (malignancy/diverticulitis) top the differential.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Free subdiaphragmatic gas signifies hollow viscus perforation, chiefly from perforated peptic ulcer disease or perforated colonic malignancy/diverticulitis.

sourceStation.title: Pneumoperitoneum on Erect CXR
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2)

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum). Causes: Perforated peptic (duodenal/gastric) ulcer, Bowel perforation (malignancy, diverticulitis, ruptured appendix), Trauma.

stem: A 42-year-old man with chronic constipation presents to casualty with severe, unremitting anal pain and an irreducible, tense, dark-purple perianal mass with surface bleeding for 24 hours, as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis and the definitive surgical procedure indicated if severe pain or impending necrosis persists within 48–72 hours?
options: Intersphincteric perianal abscess; loop colostomy formation
Full-thickness rectal prolapse; laparoscopic ventral rectopexy
Thrombosed prolapsed haemorrhoid; urgent haemorrhoidectomy
Chronic posterior anal fissure; botulinum toxin injection
Perianal squamous carcinoma; inguinal lymph node dissection
optionRationales: Incorrect: An abscess presents as a fluctuant, erythematous perianal swelling requiring simple incision and drainage rather than faecal diversion.
Incorrect: Full-thickness rectal prolapse shows concentric mucosal rings rather than an isolated engorged, thrombosed vascular cushion.

Correct: A tense, irreducible, purplish haemorrhoidal mass indicates an acute thrombosed/strangulated prolapsed haemorrhoid; within 48–72 hours of severe pain or gangrene, urgent surgical haemorrhoidectomy provides definitive relief.
Incorrect: Anal fissures present with tearing pain on defaecation and a sentinel skin tag rather than a large irreducible dark congested vascular mass.
Incorrect: Perianal squamous cell carcinoma develops slowly as an indurated ulcerating plaque rather than an acute 24-hour painful thrombosed swelling.
clinicalPearl: Acute thrombosed prolapsed haemorrhoids presenting within 48–72 hours with severe pain or necrosis benefit from urgent haemorrhoidectomy; late (>72 h) resolving cases are managed conservatively with analgesia, sitz baths, and stool softeners.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Acute thrombosed prolapsed haemorrhoids require pain control and stool softeners, with urgent haemorrhoidectomy reserved for severe pain or strangulation within 48–72 hours.

sourceStation.title: Prolapsed Thrombosed Haemorrhoid
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
09.
9.1 What is the most likely cause?
9.2 What is the most appropriate next step in the management?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (9.1) Thrombosed / strangulated prolapsed internal (or external) haemorrhoid. (9.2) Management: Analgesia, stool softeners, ice packs/warm sitz baths, and rest; if presenting acutely within 48–72 hours with severe pain/gangrene, perform urgent surgical haemorrhoidectomy (or clot evacuation under local anaesthesia for external thrombosed perianal haematoma).

stem: An 18-year-old male undergoing diagnostic laparoscopy for left upper quadrant pain is found to have gross splenomegaly with surface nodularity and cystic changes, as shown. Which pair of peripheral blood smear findings would specifically reflect chronic haemolytic disease or functional hyposplenism in this patient?
options: Auer rods and circulating myeloblasts
Howell-Jolly bodies and erythrocyte target cells
Hypersegmented neutrophils and macro-ovalocytes
Smudge cells and mature lymphocytosis
Rouleaux formation and circulating plasma cells
optionRationales: Incorrect: Auer rods inside myeloblasts are pathognomonic for acute myeloid leukaemia rather than functional hyposplenism or haemolytic anaemia.

Correct: Target cells (seen in thalassaemia/haemoglobinopathies causing splenomegaly) and Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants cleared by a functioning spleen) classically appear on the blood film in haemolytic/hyposplenic states.
Incorrect: Hypersegmented neutrophils and macro-ovalocytes are characteristic of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency (megaloblastic anaemia).
Incorrect: Smudge (basket) cells with mature lymphocytosis are typical of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
Incorrect: Marked rouleaux formation with circulating plasma cells points toward multiple myeloma rather than splenic haemolytic or hyposplenic pathology.
clinicalPearl: Always correlate surgical splenomegaly with the peripheral blood picture: target cells, reticulocytosis, and Howell-Jolly bodies signal underlying haemoglobinopathy or functional hyposplenism.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Splenomegaly and post-splenectomy states require peripheral blood film review for target cells, reticulocytes, and Howell-Jolly bodies reflecting haemolysis or hyposplenism.

sourceStation.title: Splenomegaly / Splenic Cysts (Laparoscopy)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
10. 18-year-old boy presented to hospital with abdominal pain; on investigations the left upper quadrant of the abdomen shows the following finding (laparoscopic view).
10.1 What is the abnormal finding of the investigation?
10.2 Mention 2 features of the blood picture of this patient.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (10.1) Gross splenomegaly (with splenic cysts/nodularity/infarcts). (10.2) Blood picture features (reflecting underlying haemolytic anaemia or hyposplenism): Target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies (if functional hyposplenism/post-splenectomy), Spherocytes / sickle cells / microcytic hypochromic cells, Reticulocytosis / polychromasia.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids. Upper GI endoscopy identifies a mid-oesophageal malignant lesion, and staging CT reveals distant metastases. Fifteen years ago he suffered accidental corrosive lye ingestion. Which histological type and pair of commonest visceral metastatic sites are expected?
options: Adenocarcinoma; spleen and kidneys
Gastrointestinal stromal tumour; pancreas and pleura
Small cell carcinoma; myocardium and thyroid gland
Squamous cell carcinoma; liver and lungs
MALT lymphoma; brain and testes
optionRationales: Incorrect: Oesophageal adenocarcinoma arises predominantly in the distal third from Barrett's oesophagus and gastro-oesophageal reflux rather than post-corrosive mid-oesophageal strictures.
Incorrect: GISTs are mesenchymal submucosal tumours unrelated to caustic stricture carcinogenesis and spread mainly to liver and peritoneum.
Incorrect: Primary oesophageal small cell carcinoma is rare and does not preferentially metastasise to myocardium and thyroid.
Correct: Prior corrosive lye ingestion confers up to a 1000-fold lifetime risk of mid-oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, which spreads haematogenously most commonly to the liver and lungs.
Incorrect: Gastric MALT lymphoma is linked to Helicobacter pylori infection rather than caustic oesophageal strictures.
clinicalPearl: A history of caustic ingestion decades earlier strongly predisposes to mid-oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma; always evaluate liver and lungs on staging CT.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Post-corrosive strictures predispose to mid-oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, requiring staging imaging focused on the liver and lungs.

sourceStation.title: Oesophageal Carcinoma Post-Corrosive Ingestion
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
5. A man presented with progressive dysphagia. He has a past history of corrosive ingestion 15 years back. His mother has breast carcinoma. He is on oral hypoglycaemics. UGIE showed a mid-oesophageal lesion; biopsy showed oesophageal carcinoma. CT scan showed distant metastases.
5.1 Give 2 facts from history that would have contributed to oesophageal carcinoma.
5.2 Give 2 histological types of oesophageal cancer.
5.3 Give 2 most likely distant metastasis sites.  [Text-only station in original PPTX]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (5.1) Risk factors: Past corrosive ingestion (lye stricture — 1000-fold increased risk of SCC) and family history of malignancy (or male sex/metabolic syndrome/GERD in DM). (5.2) Histological types: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) (classic in mid-oesophagus & post-corrosive) and Adenocarcinoma. (5.3) Distant metastasis sites: Liver and Lungs (also non-regional lymph nodes, bone, adrenals).

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with acute, severe upper abdominal pain, as illustrated. While urgent ECG, serum amylase, and erect chest radiography are arranged to exclude perforated peptic ulcer, acute pancreatitis, acute cholecystitis, and inferior myocardial infarction, which analgesic regimen is safest and most effective for immediate relief?
options: Titrated intravenous morphine with an antiemetic plus IV paracetamol
High-dose oral ibuprofen tablets combined with oral codeine phosphate
Intramuscular diclofenac bolus prior to renal and ulcer exclusion
Withholding all analgesia completely until diagnostic laparotomy finishes
Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate spray with loading oral aspirin tablets
optionRationales: Correct: Early titrated IV morphine (2–5 mg with an antiemetic) combined with IV paracetamol (1 g) provides effective, safe analgesia in severe acute abdominal pain without masking true peritoneal signs or risking ulcer bleeding.
Incorrect: Oral medications are poorly absorbed in acute abdominal emergencies (especially with vomiting/ileus), and oral NSAIDs risk severe worsening if a perforated peptic ulcer is present.
Incorrect: Parenteral NSAIDs such as diclofenac should be avoided until peptic ulcer perforation, GI haemorrhage, and acute kidney injury have been ruled out.
Incorrect: Withholding analgesia is outdated and inhumane; titrated IV opioids facilitate physical examination without obscuring genuine peritonism.
Incorrect: Aspirin is hazardous if upper GI ulceration or perforation is present, and GTN does not address surgical causes of acute upper abdominal pain.
clinicalPearl: Never withhold analgesia in acute abdomen: titrated IV morphine (with antiemetic) plus IV paracetamol is safe, whereas NSAIDs must wait until peptic ulcer and renal impairment are excluded.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Pain control follows the WHO analgesic ladder; NSAIDs are contraindicated when peptic ulcer risk or renal impairment is present, favouring titrated IV opioids and IV paracetamol.

sourceStation.title: Acute Severe Upper Abdominal Pain & Analgesia
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
7. A 55-year-old male presented with acute, severe, upper abdominal pain.
7.1 Give three (03) possible causes for this pain.
7.2 Name two (02) drugs used for his pain relief with their routes of administration.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (7.1) Causes: Acute pancreatitis, Perforated peptic ulcer, Acute cholecystitis / biliary colic, Acute myocardial infarction (inferior), Ruptured AAA / Mesenteric ischaemia. (7.2) Analgesics & routes: (1) IV Morphine (titrated slowly, 2–5 mg IV with antiemetic) or IV/IM Pethidine / Fentanyl; (2) IV Paracetamol (1 g IV 6-hourly) or PR Diclofenac (100 mg suppository, only if renal function normal & no PUD/bleeding risk).

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with altered bowel habits and anaemia. Colonoscopy reveals the friable, polypoidal malignant tumour shown in the ascending colon, confirmed as adenocarcinoma on biopsy without distant metastases on staging CT. What is the definitive surgical resection of choice?
options: Anterior resection with total mesorectal excision
Abdominoperineal resection with permanent end colostomy
Hartmann's procedure with descending end colostomy
Endoscopic mucosal resection without lymphadenectomy
Right hemicolectomy and primary ileocolic anastomosis
optionRationales: Incorrect: Anterior resection removes mid/upper rectal and distal sigmoid tumours rather than right-sided ascending colon malignancies.
Incorrect: Abdominoperineal resection is indicated for very low rectal cancers involving the anal sphincter.
Incorrect: Hartmann's procedure resects the rectosigmoid colon and leaves a rectal stump, typically in emergency left-sided obstruction or perforation.
Incorrect: Endoscopic mucosal resection is reserved for superficial T1/dysplastic polyps and cannot provide adequate regional mesenteric lymph node clearance for invasive adenocarcinoma.

Correct: Curative surgical resection for ascending colon adenocarcinoma requires a right hemicolectomy (resecting terminal ileum, caecum, ascending colon, and proximal transverse colon along the ileocolic and right colic vessels) with ileocolic anastomosis.
clinicalPearl: Colonic adenocarcinoma resections follow lymphatic and arterial supply: ascending colon tumours require right hemicolectomy with ileocolic/right colic pedicle ligation.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Resection of right-sided colonic adenocarcinoma (right hemicolectomy) requires bowel preparation or ERAS protocol, stoma counselling, and IV cefuroxime plus metronidazole at induction.

sourceStation.title: Ascending Colon Adenocarcinoma (Colonoscopy)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Question 01
A 50-year-old male presented with altered bowel habits and underwent a colonoscopy where a malignant tumour was detected in the ascending colon.
1.1 List 3 features of the lesion which you would include in the endoscopy report. (6 marks)
1.2 What is the most probable histological type of this lesion? (2 marks)
1.3 What is definitive surgery in the management of this patient? (2 marks)
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1.1) Features: Polypoidal tumour protruding into lumen, light pink/friable appearance, irregular margin of attachment / surface ulceration. (1.2) Histology: Adenocarcinoma. (1.3) Definitive surgery: Right hemicolectomy.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with refractory immune thrombocytopenia is scheduled for elective surgical removal of the organ circled and labelled 'A' on the diagram. Which specific preoperative precaution must be completed at least 2 weeks before surgery to prevent overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis?
options: Fourteen-day course of oral metronidazole and ciprofloxacin
Preoperative radioiodine ablation of accessory parenchyma
Vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Hib
Mechanical bowel preparation using four sachets of PEG
Intravenous vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma infusion
optionRationales: Incorrect: Empirical preoperative broad-spectrum oral antibiotics do not confer long-term protection against encapsulated organisms post-splenectomy.
Incorrect: Radioiodine ablation applies to thyroid disorders, not splenic haematological surgery.

Correct: Vaccinating against encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b) at least 2 weeks prior to elective splenectomy maximises humoral immunity and prevents fatal overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis.
Incorrect: Mechanical bowel preparation with PEG is specific to colorectal procedures and colonoscopy, not elective splenectomy.
Incorrect: Vitamin K and FFP correct coagulopathy rather than preventing post-splenectomy bacterial sepsis.
clinicalPearl: Elective splenectomy mandates vaccination against encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae type b) ≥2 weeks preoperatively, plus post-op antibiotic prophylaxis.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Elective splenectomy requires specific preoperative immunisation against encapsulated organisms at least 2 weeks before surgery to prevent overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis.

sourceStation.title: Elective Splenectomy — Complications & Pre-op Prophylaxis
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Question 02
2.1 What is the organ indicated by letter A? (2 marks)
2.2 List 3 complications specific to elective removal of this organ. (6 marks)
2.3 Name one preoperative precaution specific for this surgery. (2 marks)
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (2.1) Spleen. (2.2) Complications: Overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis (OPSS), Portal/splenic vein thrombosis, Subphrenic abscess, Reactionary haemorrhage/haematoma, Injury to pancreatic tail (acute pancreatitis / pancreatic fistula), Splenosis. (2.3) Pre-op precaution: Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type b) at least 2 weeks before elective surgery (plus lifelong/prophylactic penicillin V as per protocol).

stem: A 40-year-old man with chronic alcohol misuse presents with recurrent severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and marked weight loss. His plain abdominal radiograph is shown. Which clinical triad most characteristically accompanies the diagnosis indicated by the arrows?
options: Painless obstructive jaundice, pale stools, and palpable gallbladder
Chronic epigastric pain, malabsorptive steatorrhoea, and diabetes
Colicky abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, and absolute constipation
Right upper quadrant pain, spiking fever, and shaking rigors
Early satiety, projectile non-bilious vomiting, and succussion splash
optionRationales: Incorrect: Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law) suggests periampullary or pancreatic head carcinoma rather than chronic calcific pancreatitis.

Correct: Multiple speckled pancreatic calcifications across L1–L2 confirm chronic calcific pancreatitis, classically presenting with the triad of chronic pancreatic pain, exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhoea), and endocrine insufficiency (diabetes mellitus).
Incorrect: Colicky pain, bilious vomiting, and absolute constipation define mechanical intestinal obstruction.
Incorrect: Right upper quadrant pain, fever, and rigors form Charcot's triad of acute ascending cholangitis (with jaundice).
Incorrect: Non-bilious vomiting with a succussion splash points to gastric outlet obstruction rather than pancreatic parenchymal calcification.
clinicalPearl: Pancreatic calcifications crossing the midline at L1–L2 on a plain X-ray are pathognomonic for chronic calcific pancreatitis—look for pain, steatorrhoea, and secondary brittle diabetes.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Chronic calcific pancreatitis causes endocrine insufficiency (diabetes mellitus) requiring preoperative HbA1c and glycaemic optimisation prior to surgical intervention.

sourceStation.title: Chronic Calcific Pancreatitis — Abdominal X-Ray
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
05. A 40-year-old male presents with chronic abdominal pain and weight loss. The X-ray is shown.
5.1 What is the abnormality shown by the arrows?
5.2 State the condition.
5.3 State three clinical features of this condition.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (5.1) Multiple pancreatic calcifications across the head, body, and tail (L1–L2). (5.2) Condition: Chronic calcific pancreatitis. (5.3) Clinical features: Chronic epigastric pain radiating to back (relieved by leaning forward), Steatorrhoea (exocrine pancreatic insufficiency), Diabetes mellitus (endocrine insufficiency / brittle DM), Significant weight loss/malnutrition.

stem: A 55-year-old man who underwent liver transplantation 3 years ago presents with dysphagia and odynophagia. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrates the diffuse white mucosal plaques shown. Which causative organism and precipitating medication regimen best explain this presentation?
options: Candida albicans; calcineurin inhibitors and corticosteroids
Helicobacter pylori; high-dose oral proton pump inhibitors
Clostridioides difficile; oral lactulose and rifaximin
Cytomegalovirus; loop diuretics and non-selective beta-blockers
Aspergillus fumigatus; ursodeoxycholic acid monotherapy
optionRationales: Correct: White adherent oesophageal plaques in a solid-organ transplant recipient are classic for Candida albicans oesophagitis triggered by maintenance immunosuppression (tacrolimus/ciclosporin, mycophenolate, and corticosteroids).
Incorrect: Helicobacter pylori colonises gastric mucosa causing gastritis and peptic ulceration rather than white oesophageal plaques.
Incorrect: Clostridioides difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis in the colon rather than upper GI oesophageal plaques.
Incorrect: CMV oesophagitis produces deep punched-out linear ulcers rather than raised creamy plaques, and diuretics/beta-blockers do not cause opportunistic fungal infection.
Incorrect: Ursodeoxycholic acid is non-immunosuppressive and does not predispose to oesophageal candidiasis.
clinicalPearl: Creamy white plaques coating the oesophagus in an immunocompromised transplant or steroid-treated patient signify oesophageal candidiasis, treated with systemic fluconazole.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Post-transplant immunosuppression (calcineurin inhibitors and corticosteroids) predisposes to opportunistic Candida albicans oesophagitis presenting as dysphagia on upper GI endoscopy.

sourceStation.title: Oesophageal Candidiasis Post-Liver Transplant
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
4.1 A 55-year-old male presented with dysphagia a few years after liver transplantation. What is the likely organism that causes the condition found in the endoscopy below?
4.2 What medication could have led to this?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (4.1) Organism: Candida albicans (oesophageal candidiasis). (4.2) Precipitating medications: Immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, ciclosporin, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine) and corticosteroids (prednisolone) required after liver transplantation (also broad-spectrum antibiotics).

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with heat intolerance, palpitations, increased sweating, and weight loss despite an increased appetite. Her facial photograph is shown. Which additional physical examination finding specifically supports the autoimmune cause of her thyrotoxicosis rather than toxic multinodular goitre?
options: Hard, fixed solitary thyroid nodule with cervical lymphadenopathy
Midline subhyoid cyst elevating on tongue protrusion
Asymmetrical nodular goitre with tracheal deviation and absent bruit
Diffuse smooth goitre with a systolic bruit and pretibial myxoedema
Bradycardia with hung-up ankle reflexes and periorbital puffiness
optionRationales: Incorrect: A hard, fixed solitary nodule with lymphadenopathy suggests thyroid carcinoma rather than autoimmune Graves' disease.
Incorrect: A midline subhyoid lump moving on tongue protrusion describes a thyroglossal duct cyst, not Graves' thyrotoxicosis.
Incorrect: An asymmetrical nodular goitre without bruit or ophthalmopathy favours toxic multinodular goitre rather than Graves' disease.

Correct: Graves' disease is uniquely characterised by TSH-receptor autoantibodies causing ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos/lid retraction as shown), a diffuse vascular goitre with an audible bruit, and pretibial myxoedema.
Incorrect: Bradycardia, delayed-relaxation ankle jerks, and myxoedematous puffiness indicate hypothyroidism rather than thyrotoxicosis.
clinicalPearl: Exophthalmos, pretibial myxoedema, and a diffuse goitre with an audible bruit distinguish autoimmune Graves' disease from other causes of thyrotoxicosis.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Patients with Graves' thyrotoxicosis require preoperative thyroid function testing and medical euthyroid optimisation before elective thyroidectomy.

sourceStation.title: Graves' Thyrotoxicosis
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Q.3
A 30-year-old female with recent-onset increased sweating and weight loss despite increased appetite presents to you.
A.) What is the diagnosis?
B.) List 4 specific physical signs you would observe in this condition on her physical examination.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (A) Graves' disease / Thyrotoxicosis. (B) Physical signs: Fine resting tremor of outstretched hands, Warm sweaty palms, Resting tachycardia / atrial fibrillation, Diffuse smooth goitre with thyroid bruit, Exophthalmos, lid lag, and lid retraction, Pretibial myxoedema, Thyroid acropachy.

stem: A child presents with the painless, smooth midline neck swelling shown, located just below the hyoid bone, which moves upward on both swallowing and tongue protrusion. Before performing a Sistrunk excision, which imaging combination is essential to exclude an ectopic thyroid gland as the sole functioning thyroid tissue?
options: Fine-needle aspiration cytology alone without neck imaging
Lateral soft-tissue radiograph of the cervical spine
Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the aortic arch
Barium swallow with videofluoroscopic manometry
Ultrasound neck and Tc-99m radioisotope thyroid scan
optionRationales: Incorrect: Cytology alone cannot confirm whether normal orthotopic thyroid lobes are present in the lower neck.
Incorrect: Plain cervical radiographs cannot reliably distinguish cystic remnants from functioning ectopic thyroid tissue.
Incorrect: CT angiography evaluates major vessels rather than thyroid embryological tissue distribution.
Incorrect: Barium swallow assesses oesophageal motility and lumen, not midline congenital neck cysts.

Correct: Ultrasound of the neck confirms a normal orthotopic thyroid gland in the lower neck, and a Tc-99m (or I-123) radioisotope scan verifies whether the midline mass is sole functioning ectopic thyroid tissue—preventing inadvertent lifelong hypothyroidism.
clinicalPearl: Never excise a midline neck swelling moving with tongue protrusion without first confirming an orthotopic thyroid gland on ultrasound/radioisotope scan, lest you remove a lingual/ectopic thyroid.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Preoperative condition-specific assessment (ultrasound and thyroid imaging) confirms normal orthotopic thyroid tissue before excising a thyroglossal cyst.

sourceStation.title: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
02. Picture of a midline neck lump (thyroglossal cyst).
What is the diagnosis? How do you differentiate it from an ectopic thyroid?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Thyroglossal cyst (clinically moves upward with both swallowing AND tongue protrusion). Differentiate from ectopic thyroid: By radiological imaging — Ultrasound neck (confirms presence of a normal orthotopic thyroid gland in the lower neck) and Radioisotope thyroid scan (Tc-99m / I-123) before excision (removing an ectopic thyroid if no normal gland exists causes lifelong hypothyroidism!).

stem: During preoperative assessment for an elective cholecystectomy, a 58-year-old clinically euthyroid woman has thyroid function tests showing a suppressed serum TSH (<0.05 mIU/L) with serum free T3 and free T4 concentrations within the normal reference range. What is the most accurate biochemical diagnosis?
options: Overt primary hyperthyroidism
Subclinical hyperthyroidism
Subclinical hypothyroidism
Secondary central hypothyroidism
Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis)
optionRationales: Incorrect: Overt primary hyperthyroidism requires elevated free T4 and/or free T3 in addition to a suppressed TSH.
Correct: A suppressed serum TSH alongside normal circulating free T3 and free T4 defines subclinical hyperthyroidism.
Incorrect: Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined by an elevated TSH with normal free T4 and free T3.
Incorrect: Secondary (central) hypothyroidism features a low free T4 accompanied by a low or inappropriately normal TSH.
Incorrect: Thyroid storm is a life-threatening clinical decompensation with overt thyrotoxicosis rather than an asymptomatic euthyroid screening result.
clinicalPearl: Suppressed TSH + normal free T3/T4 = subclinical hyperthyroidism; elevated TSH + normal free T4 = subclinical hypothyroidism.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Condition-specific preoperative thyroid function tests identify subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH with normal T3/T4) that warrants atrial fibrillation and anaesthetic risk review.

sourceStation.title: Subclinical Hyperthyroidism
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
04. Thyroid function test result: TSH low, T3 and T4 normal.
What is the diagnosis?  [Text-only station]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Subclinical hyperthyroidism.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a pre-existing, non-progressive lump on his lower neck that recently became painful, swollen, warm, and erythematous, as shown. Which two-stage management strategy is most appropriate?
options: Immediate primary elliptical excision and tight subcuticular skin closure
Simple needle aspiration followed by intralesional corticosteroid injection
Antibiotics plus drainage if abscessed, then elective cyst wall excision
Warm compresses alone with permanent discharge and no future excision
Wide radical excision with 2 cm margins and ipsilateral lymphadenectomy
optionRationales: Incorrect: Excising an acutely inflamed cyst risks wound dehiscence, infection spread, and incomplete removal of the friable cyst wall leading to recurrence.
Incorrect: Intralesional steroid injection is used for keloids or inflammatory dermatoses, not an acutely infected epidermoid abscess.

Correct: An infected sebaceous (epidermoid) cyst requires antibiotics (± incision and drainage if pus has formed), followed by definitive surgical excision of the entire cyst wall and punctum once acute inflammation resolves.
Incorrect: Leaving the intact epithelial lining behind guarantees recurrent infection once antibiotics stop.
Incorrect: Wide oncological excision and lymphadenectomy are unwarranted for a benign cutaneous epidermoid cyst.
clinicalPearl: Never attempt definitive primary excision of an acutely infected sebaceous cyst; drain/treat infection first, then excise the entire capsule and punctum electively to prevent recurrence.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Infected cysts undergo casualty incision and drainage (using the I&D packet with No. 3 BP handle and sinus forceps) followed by elective excision once inflammation settles.

sourceStation.title: Infected Sebaceous (Epidermoid) Cyst
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
3. A 45-year-old man presented to the surgery clinic with a lump in neck/back. Patient complains that it is very painful and tender, and is non-progressive. On examination, it was red and warm (central punctum).
1. What is your diagnosis?
2. List 3 features of acute inflammation of this lump.
3. What is the best treatment for this condition?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Infected sebaceous (epidermoid) cyst. (2) Features of acute inflammation: Redness (rubor), Warmth (calor), Pain/tenderness (dolor), Swelling (tumor). (3) Treatment: Initial antibiotics ± incision & drainage if abscess formed; complete surgical excision (including cyst wall & punctum) once acute inflammation has settled to prevent recurrence.

stem: On the first postoperative day after a total thyroidectomy for Graves' disease, a 35-year-old woman develops circumoral numbness and tingling of her hands and feet. Inflating a blood pressure cuff on her upper arm above systolic pressure induces the hand posture shown. What is this sign and the responsible biochemical abnormality?
options: Trousseau's sign; hypocalcaemia from hypoparathyroidism
Chvostek's sign; hyperkalaemia from tissue necrosis
Pemberton's sign; hypomagnesaemia with metabolic alkalosis
Froment's sign; acute ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow
Phalen's sign; postoperative hypercalcaemic crisis
optionRationales: Correct: Carpopedal spasm (wrist and MCP flexion, IP extension, thumb adduction) provoked by brachial artery cuff occlusion is Trousseau's sign, caused by acute post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia from parathyroid gland ischaemia or inadvertent excision.
Incorrect: Chvostek's sign is ipsilateral facial muscle twitching elicited by tapping the facial nerve anterior to the tragus, and hyperkalaemia does not cause carpopedal spasm.
Incorrect: Pemberton's sign is facial plethora and venous engorgement on arm elevation in retrosternal goitre causing thoracic inlet obstruction.
Incorrect: Froment's sign tests adductor pollicis weakness in ulnar neuropathy, not hypocalcaemic tetany.
Incorrect: Phalen's sign evaluates median nerve compression in carpal tunnel syndrome, not acute hypocalcaemia.
clinicalPearl: Trousseau's sign (carpopedal spasm with BP cuff inflation) is more specific than Chvostek's sign for post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia; severe tetany or stridor requires immediate IV calcium gluconate.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Hypocalcaemia is a key early post-thyroidectomy complication presenting with circumoral paraesthesia, Trousseau's sign, and Chvostek's sign.

sourceStation.title: Trousseau's Sign (Post-Thyroidectomy Hypocalcaemia)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
4) A 35-year-old lady who underwent total thyroidectomy for Graves' disease developed circumoral numbness and tingling sensation over the hands and feet the following day. On examination, the following sign was elicited.
1) What is the sign?
2) Name one other sign to confirm the diagnosis of the above sign.
3) What is the biochemical abnormality in this patient?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Trousseau's sign (carpopedal spasm: flexion of wrist & MCP joints, extension of IP joints, thumb adduction). (2) Other sign: Chvostek's sign (ipsilateral facial muscle twitching on tapping facial nerve anterior to tragus). (3) Biochemical abnormality: Hypocalcaemia (secondary to transient/permanent hypoparathyroidism).

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with the left breast changes shown in the photograph, including nipple inversion and adjacent skin dimpling. As part of formal triple assessment, which initial radiological investigation is indicated alongside clinical examination and core needle biopsy?
options: Contrast-enhanced CT thorax and upper abdomen
Whole-body FDG positron emission tomography (PET-CT)
Plain anteroposterior chest radiograph and thoracic views
Bilateral diagnostic mammography with breast ultrasound
Technetium-99m whole-body bone scintigraphy scan
optionRationales: Incorrect: CT thorax/abdomen is used for systemic staging after histological confirmation of invasive malignancy, not as the initial breast diagnostic study.
Incorrect: Whole-body PET-CT is reserved for complex staging or recurrence evaluation rather than first-line breast imaging.
Incorrect: Chest radiography cannot image breast parenchymal microcalcifications or mass architecture.

Correct: At age ≥40 years, bilateral diagnostic mammography (often paired with targeted breast ultrasound) is the initial gold-standard radiological arm of triple assessment for suspected breast carcinoma.
Incorrect: Bone scintigraphy screens for osseous metastases post-diagnosis rather than evaluating a primary breast lesion.
clinicalPearl: Triple assessment = clinical exam + breast imaging (mammography ± ultrasound in ≥40 yrs; ultrasound alone in <35 yrs) + core biopsy/FNAC.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Diagnostic confirmation precedes surgical planning; women ≥40 with nipple retraction and skin tethering undergo bilateral mammography plus breast ultrasound within triple assessment.

sourceStation.title: Left Breast Carcinoma (Nipple Retraction & Skin Dimpling)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
1. 45-year-old female presented with left breast changes as shown.
1.1 List 2 abnormal physical signs that can be seen.
1.2 What is the most likely diagnosis?
1.3 What is the most suitable initial radiological investigation?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1.1) Abnormal signs: Left nipple retraction/inversion and skin dimpling / tethering (peau d'orange/asymmetry). (1.2) Diagnosis: Left breast carcinoma. (1.3) Initial radiology: Bilateral Mammography (gold standard at age ≥ 40; combine with Breast Ultrasound as part of Triple Assessment).

stem: A woman presents with the large anterior neck swelling shown in the photograph. Which combination of bedside clinical sign and initial radiological plus tissue investigations appropriately confirms thyroid involvement and evaluates the mass?
options: Moves upward on tongue protrusion; CT chest and open incisional biopsy
Remains fixed on swallowing; cervical spine X-ray and punch biopsy
Displays expansile pulsation; carotid angiography and bone marrow biopsy
Transilluminates brightly; barium swallow and excisional lymph node biopsy
Moves upward with swallowing only; thyroid ultrasound and targeted FNAC
optionRationales: Incorrect: Upward movement on tongue protrusion indicates a thyroglossal duct cyst rather than a thyroid goitre, and open biopsy is avoided initially.
Incorrect: Thyroid swellings move upward with swallowing via the pretracheal fascia unless fixed by advanced anaplastic invasion; plain X-ray and punch skin biopsy are inappropriate.
Incorrect: Expansile pulsation points to carotid aneurysm/vascular pathology rather than goitre.
Incorrect: Brilliant transillumination is characteristic of cystic hygroma rather than solid/multinodular thyroid goitre.

Correct: Pretracheal fascial attachment causes a thyroid goitre to rise on swallowing while staying stationary on tongue protrusion; first-line evaluation pairs thyroid ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC).
clinicalPearl: Swallowing moves both thyroid goitres and thyroglossal cysts upward, whereas tongue protrusion specifically moves thyroglossal cysts; ultrasound + FNAC are first-line investigations for thyroid nodules.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Thyroid swellings are evaluated with condition-specific TFTs, neck ultrasound, and fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) prior to surgical planning.

sourceStation.title: Goitre — Examination & Initial Investigations
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2. A lady as shown in the picture presents with a neck lump suspected to be goitre.
• List 2 physical signs to elicit to confirm that this is a goitre.
• Name the suitable initial investigation for: (1) Radiological, (2) Tissue diagnosis.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (3.1) Signs confirming goitre: (a) Moves upward on swallowing (due to pretracheal fascia attachment to larynx); (b) Non-mobile on tongue protrusion (differentiates from thyroglossal cyst); check ability to get below lower border (excludes retrosternal extension) and palpate from behind. (3.2) Investigations: Radiological = Thyroid Ultrasound (USS); Tissue diagnosis = Fine-Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC).

stem: A 50-year-old non-lactating woman presents with fever and a tender, erythematous swelling of the right breast, as shown. Her symptoms settle after ultrasound-guided aspiration and oral co-amoxiclav. Which essential follow-up step must be scheduled once the acute inflammation resolves?
options: Reassurance and discharge once skin erythema completely fades
Repeat clinical exam, diagnostic mammography, and core biopsy
Routine bilateral prophylactic simple mastectomy for duct ectasia
Empirical 6-month antituberculous therapy without tissue biopsy
Serial serum prolactin and CA-125 monitoring every 3 months
optionRationales: Incorrect: Discharging a 50-year-old non-lactating woman without post-resolution imaging risks missing an underlying or inflammatory breast carcinoma masquerading as mastitis.

Correct: Non-lactational mastitis or breast abscess in women ≥40 years warrants post-resolution triple assessment—clinical re-examination, diagnostic mammography/ultrasound, and core biopsy of any residual mass or thickening—to exclude malignancy.
Incorrect: Mastectomy is never indicated prophylactically for uncomplicated resolved mastitis without proven cancer.
Incorrect: Tuberculous mastitis requires microbiological or histological proof before commencing antituberculous therapy.
Incorrect: Prolactin and CA-125 have no role in ruling out breast carcinoma after mastitis.
clinicalPearl: In any non-lactating woman over 40 presenting with mastitis or breast abscess, always perform post-resolution triple assessment (mammography ± biopsy) to exclude inflammatory breast cancer.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Suspicious breast lesions require definitive tissue and radiological exclusion of malignancy prior to concluding benign follow-up.

sourceStation.title: Acute Mastitis / Breast Abscess
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
14. 50-year-old female with right breast pain, tenderness, and fever.
14.1 What is the clinical diagnosis?
14.2 What is the probable treatment option given?
14.3 Mention how to follow up this patient.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (14.1) Acute mastitis / Breast abscess (note: in a 50yo non-lactating woman, must exclude inflammatory breast carcinoma and periductal mastitis). (14.2) Treatment: Empirical anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (e.g., Flucloxacillin / Co-amoxiclav) + analgesics; if fluctuant/abscess on USS → USS-guided needle aspiration (or surgical incision & drainage) with pus culture. (14.3) Follow-up: Triple assessment after resolution — clinical breast re-examination + mammography/USS and core biopsy if any residual mass/thickening persists, to rule out underlying breast malignancy.

stem: A 38-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma, yielding the specimen shown with a prominent midline superior projection arising from the isthmus. Leaving this embryological remnant behind during total thyroidectomy most significantly increases the risk of which postoperative problem?
options: Immediate bilateral vocal cord paralysis from nerve trauma
Permanent hypocalcaemia from parathyroid gland infarction
Local tumour recurrence and impaired radioiodine ablation
Acute intraoperative carotid artery air embolism
Chylothorax from left-sided thoracic duct laceration
optionRationales: Incorrect: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy results from dissection injury near the tracheo-oesophageal groove/Berry's ligament, not failure to excise the midline pyramidal lobe.
Incorrect: Hypoparathyroidism arises from devascularisation or removal of the posterior parathyroid glands rather than retaining an anterior pyramidal lobe.

Correct: Failure to excise the pyramidal lobe and thyroglossal tract remnant leaves functional thyroid tissue behind, increasing local recurrence in thyroid cancer (or Graves' relapse) and trapping postoperative radioiodine.
Incorrect: Air embolism is an anaesthetic/central-line or open major neck vein hazard unrelated to retained thyroid embryological remnants.
Incorrect: Thoracic duct injury is a complication of left-sided level IV lateral neck dissection rather than midline pyramidal lobe retention.
clinicalPearl: Always inspect the superior border of the thyroid isthmus and trace up to the hyoid during total thyroidectomy to remove the pyramidal lobe and thyroglossal tract completely.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Incomplete removal of embryological thyroid remnants (pyramidal lobe/thyroglossal tract) risks local cancer recurrence, Graves' relapse, and avid uptake interfering with radioiodine ablation.

sourceStation.title: Total Thyroidectomy Specimen — Embryological Remnants
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
15. Photograph of a total thyroidectomy specimen is given.
15.1 Identify two (02) embryological remnants of the thyroid gland that are seen in this specimen.
15.2 State two (02) complications that arise when these remnants are left behind during total thyroidectomy.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (15.1) Embryological remnants: Pyramidal lobe and Thyroglossal tract / duct remnant (or Zuckerkandl tubercle). (15.2) Complications if left behind: (a) Incomplete tumour clearance / local recurrence in differentiated thyroid cancer; (b) Recurrent hyperthyroidism (Graves' relapse); (c) Development of a thyroglossal cyst / fistula or remnant hypertrophy complicating radioiodine ablation.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a painful, warm, erythematous, and fluctuant breast lump for 4 days, as shown in the photograph. She is febrile (38.3°C) with intact overlying skin. What is the most appropriate immediate step in management?
options: Breast ultrasound with guided needle aspiration and anti-staphylococcal antibiotics
Immediate wide open surgical incision under general anaesthesia without prior imaging
Oral fluconazole monotherapy combined with topical hydrocortisone cream twice daily
Urgent wide local excision of the breast lump and axillary lymph node clearance
Tight compression bandaging and fluid restriction without antimicrobial therapy
optionRationales: Correct: Breast ultrasound confirms a drainable abscess cavity and guides needle aspiration (sending pus for culture and sensitivities) alongside empirical anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (e.g., flucloxacillin or co-amoxiclav) and analgesia.

Incorrect: USS-guided aspiration is preferred first-line over open incision and drainage when overlying skin is healthy and intact, yielding superior cosmetic results; open I&D is reserved for skin necrosis or failed aspirations.
Incorrect: Acute puerperal and non-puerperal breast abscesses are bacterial (predominantly Staphylococcus aureus/anaerobes), not fungal, and topical steroids worsen infection.
Incorrect: Urgent cancer resection is inappropriate prior to treating acute suppurative infection and obtaining tissue diagnosis.
Incorrect: Compression without drainage and antibiotics risks worsening sepsis and mammary fistula formation.
clinicalPearl: First-line management of an acute breast abscess with intact skin is ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (repeated if needed) plus anti-staphylococcal antibiotics—reserve open I&D for overlying skin necrosis.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Acute staphylococcal soft-tissue abscesses require appropriate anti-staphylococcal antibiotic therapy alongside targeted drainage and culture.

sourceStation.title: Breast Abscess — Management & Follow-Up
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
6. 45-year-old female presented with a painful, erythematous, and swollen lump on her breast.
6.1 What is the diagnosis?
6.2 What is the most appropriate next step of management?
6.3 How would you follow up this patient after the acute phase is settled?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (6.1) Breast abscess (or acute mastitis). (6.2) Next step: Ultrasound breast to confirm abscess cavity + USS-guided needle aspiration (send pus for culture/ABST) and start empirical anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (e.g., Flucloxacillin/Co-amoxiclav) + analgesia (I&D if skin necrotic or multiloculated). (6.3) Follow-up: Repeat clinical exam + mammography ± tissue biopsy (Triple assessment) once inflammation resolves, to exclude inflammatory/underlying breast carcinoma in a 45-year-old.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a painless, slow-growing lump on his upper back present for 2 years, as shown. On palpation, it is smooth, spherical, and tethered to the overlying skin. Which characteristic clinical sign and definitive treatment match this lesion?
options: Positive slip sign; simple subcutaneous lipoma enucleation
Brilliant transillumination; percutaneous doxycycline sclerotherapy
Expansile pulsation; endovascular coil embolisation procedure
Central punctum; complete elliptical excision of intact cyst wall
Fluctuance across two planes; simple stab incision and expression
optionRationales: Incorrect: The slip sign and free overlying skin mobility characterise a subcutaneous lipoma rather than a skin-tethered epidermoid cyst.
Incorrect: Sebaceous cysts contain thick keratinous material and do not transilluminate.
Incorrect: Expansile pulsation occurs in arterial aneurysms and arteriovenous malformations.

Correct: An epidermoid (sebaceous) cyst is anchored to the epidermis via a visible central punctum and requires complete surgical excision taking an elliptical skin island around the punctum with the entire cyst capsule intact.
Incorrect: Expressing cyst contents without removing the epithelial wall inevitably leads to cyst recurrence.
clinicalPearl: Cannot pinch skin over a sebaceous cyst + central punctum = epidermoid cyst; always excise the entire wall via a skin ellipse to prevent recurrence.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Uninfected sebaceous cysts are excised electively using a casualty excision-biopsy packet, removing an ellipse of skin around the central punctum and the intact cyst wall.

sourceStation.title: Sebaceous Cyst on Back
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
8. This is a lump on the back of the chest of a 45-year-old man.
8.1 What is the diagnosis?
8.2 Write two (02) specific features you would observe in this lump.
8.3 What is the definitive treatment?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (8.1) Sebaceous (epidermoid) cyst. (8.2) Specific features: Visible central punctum, tethered/attached to overlying skin (cannot pinch skin over it), smooth, spherical, fluctuant/doughy consistency. (8.3) Definitive treatment: Complete surgical excision under local anaesthesia, taking an ellipse of skin around the punctum and removing the entire cyst wall intact.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with spontaneous blood-stained nipple discharge, as shown in the photograph. Which triad of pathologies must be evaluated through formal triple assessment?
options: Fibroadenoma, simple breast cyst, and Mondor's disease
Fat necrosis, galactocoele, and benign phyllodes tumour
Accessory breast tissue, lipoma, and Tietze's syndrome
Gynaecomastia, hidradenitis suppurativa, and epidermoid cyst
Intraductal papilloma, breast cancer/DCIS, and duct ectasia
optionRationales: Incorrect: Fibroadenomas, simple cysts, and Mondor's superficial thrombophlebitis do not classically present with bloody nipple discharge.
Incorrect: Fat necrosis, galactocoele (milky fluid), and phyllodes tumour typically present as discrete breast masses rather than spontaneous bloody ductal discharge.
Incorrect: Costochondritis (Tietze's syndrome) and lipomas cause chest wall pain or subcutaneous lumps unrelated to lactiferous ducts.
Incorrect: Hidradenitis suppurativa affects apocrine skin folds rather than lactiferous ducts causing bloody nipple discharge.

Correct: Spontaneous bloody nipple discharge is most commonly caused by an intraductal papilloma, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or invasive breast carcinoma, and occasionally mammary duct ectasia—mandating complete triple assessment.
clinicalPearl: Bloody nipple discharge is intraductal papilloma until proven otherwise, but underlying DCIS/invasive carcinoma (~10–20%) and duct ectasia must always be excluded via triple assessment.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Bloody nipple discharge requires triple assessment (clinical exam, mammography/breast ultrasound, and cytology or biopsy) to rule out underlying carcinoma before surgical planning.

sourceStation.title: Bloody Multi-Duct Nipple Discharge
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
17. This is a picture of a nipple-areolar complex.
17.1 What is the clinical condition shown in the picture?
17.2 List 3 causes for this condition.
17.3 What assessments are to be done in this condition?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (17.1) Bloody nipple discharge. (17.2) Causes: Intraductal papilloma (commonest cause of single-duct bloody discharge), Breast carcinoma / DCIS, Duct ectasia (may be blood-stained/multi-duct). (17.3) Assessments: Triple assessment (full breast/axillary exam, Diagnostic mammography + Breast USS, Nipple discharge cytology / core biopsy / microdochectomy or ductoscopy as indicated).

stem: A 53-year-old woman presents with the anterior neck swelling shown alongside palpitations, nervousness, and weight loss. After confirming thyroid involvement by observing upward movement on swallowing water, which bedside physical signs specifically indicate thyrotoxicosis?
options: Sinus bradycardia, dry coarse skin, and delayed ankle reflex relaxation
Resting tachycardia, fine hand tremor, warm moist palms, and lid lag
Carpopedal spasm, circumoral paraesthesia, and positive Chvostek's sign
Absent radial pulse, Horner's syndrome, and wasted small hand muscles
Isolated facial plethora on arm elevation with normal resting heart rate
optionRationales: Incorrect: Bradycardia, dry skin, and slow-relaxing reflexes are classic features of hypothyroidism.
Correct: Sympathetic and metabolic hyperactivity in thyrotoxicosis produces resting tachycardia (or atrial fibrillation), fine resting hand tremor, warm moist palms, and lid lag/retraction.
Incorrect: Carpopedal spasm and Chvostek's sign indicate hypocalcaemia (e.g., post-thyroidectomy), not thyrotoxicosis.
Incorrect: Horner's syndrome with small-muscle hand wasting suggests Pancoast tumour or thoracic outlet compression rather than thyrotoxicosis.
Incorrect: Positive Pemberton's sign reflects mechanical thoracic inlet compression by a retrosternal goitre and can occur in a euthyroid patient.
clinicalPearl: During thyroid exam: confirm deglutition mobility first, palpate from behind, percuss over the manubrium for retrosternal extension, and check palms, pulse, tremor, and eyes for thyrotoxic status.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Thyroid examination and preoperative assessment must confirm functional thyrotoxic signs (tachycardia, tremor, lid lag) so patients are rendered euthyroid before surgery.

sourceStation.title: Thyroid Goitre & Thyrotoxic Signs
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
20. A 53-year-old lady presented at clinic with the following presentation.
20.1 What is the organ that has been involved in this presentation?
20.2 Mention how to confirm the involvement of the above organ in the clinic.
20.3 Mention 3 clinical signs that explain her hyperactivity.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (20.1) Thyroid gland. (20.2) Confirmation: Ask patient to swallow water/saliva — the lump moves upwards with deglutition. (20.3) Signs of thyrotoxic hyperactivity: Resting tachycardia / atrial fibrillation, Fine resting tremor of outstretched hands, Warm moist palms / hyperhidrosis, Lid lag / lid retraction / exophthalmos, Brisk reflexes, Proximal muscle weakness.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of unilateral itching, erythematous scaling, and intermittent blood-stained discharge affecting the left nipple-areolar complex (illustrated) that failed to respond to topical corticosteroids. Which diagnostic pair of investigations is most definitive for confirming Paget's disease of the nipple and evaluating underlying malignancy?
options: Superficial fungal skin scraping and empirical oral clotrimazole trial
Serum CA 15-3 measurement and plain anteroposterior chest radiograph
Full-thickness nipple-areolar biopsy and bilateral breast mammography
Bacterial swab of nipple discharge and repeat topical steroid course
Axillary lymph node ultrasound alone without nipple tissue sampling
optionRationales: Incorrect: Treating refractory unilateral nipple changes as eczema or fungal dermatitis delays diagnosis of underlying breast malignancy.
Incorrect: CA 15-3 is neither sensitive nor specific for diagnosing primary breast cancer or Paget's disease.

Correct: Paget's disease of the nipple is almost always associated with underlying DCIS or invasive breast carcinoma; diagnosis requires a full-thickness wedge/punch biopsy of the nipple-areolar skin alongside bilateral diagnostic mammography (and breast USS/MRI).
Incorrect: Repeating topical steroids on a unilateral steroid-resistant nipple lesion misses a crucial red flag for breast malignancy.
Incorrect: Axillary imaging alone cannot establish histology of the primary nipple-areolar lesion or detect in-situ disease.
clinicalPearl: Unilateral nipple 'eczema' failing topical steroids is Paget's disease of the nipple until biopsied—always perform a full-thickness nipple-areolar biopsy plus bilateral mammography.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Diagnostic confirmation precedes surgical therapy; refractory unilateral nipple lesions require full-thickness biopsy and bilateral mammography to detect underlying DCIS or invasive carcinoma.

sourceStation.title: Paget's Disease of the Nipple
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
01. A 55-year-old woman presents with a breast condition in her left breast as shown in the picture.
1.1 Explain the clinical symptoms/signs seen in the picture.
1.2 List three red-flag signs.
1.3 Mention two investigations.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1.1) Clinical features: Eczematous, erythematous, scaling/crusting ulceration of the nipple-areolar complex (Paget's disease of the nipple, almost always associated with underlying DCIS or invasive ductal carcinoma). (1.2) Red flags: Unilateral chronic 'eczema' failing topical steroids, nipple destruction/inversion, bloody nipple discharge, palpable breast lump, axillary lymphadenopathy. (1.3) Investigations: Full-thickness wedge/punch biopsy of nipple-areolar skin + Bilateral Mammography (and Breast USS/MRI).

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with the huge anterior neck swelling shown, whose inferior margin cannot be palpated above the manubrium sterni. Which imaging modality best defines the inferior mediastinal extent, vascular relationships, and degree of tracheal compression before surgery?
options: Contrast CT of the neck and superior mediastinum
Technetium-99m thyroid scintigraphy scan alone
Lateral plain radiograph of the cervical spine
Contrast barium swallow fluoroscopy examination
Carotid artery duplex colour Doppler ultrasound
optionRationales: Correct: When the lower border of a large goitre extends behind the sternum (unable to get below it clinically), CT of the neck and superior mediastinum accurately maps retrosternal extension, tracheal narrowing/deviation, and great vessel displacement.
Incorrect: Radioisotope scintigraphy shows functional uptake only and lacks detailed cross-sectional anatomical resolution of mediastinal structures and airway calibre.
Incorrect: Plain lateral cervical views offer limited visualisation of the superior mediastinum due to overlapping bony shoulders and sternum.
Incorrect: Barium swallow demonstrates external oesophageal indentation only and cannot evaluate tracheal lumen or mediastinal vessels.
Incorrect: Carotid duplex assesses arterial stenosis rather than retrosternal thyroid goitre depth or tracheal compression.
clinicalPearl: Inability to palpate below a goitre + dullness over the manubrium + positive Pemberton's sign = retrosternal extension; CT neck and thorax is the gold standard for preoperative surgical planning.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Mediastinal/retrosternal goitres require CT of the neck and superior mediastinum to delineate inferior thoracic extent and tracheal deviation prior to surgery.

sourceStation.title: Large Goitre — Features & Extent Imaging
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
5.1 Write down two features of the patient that you can observe.
5.2 What is the best imaging modality to identify the extent of the pathology of the above lesion?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (5.1) Features: Large midline/bilateral anterior neck swelling below thyroid cartilage, smooth/lobulated contour, asymmetrical enlargement (check if lower border is visible/palpable). (5.2) Best imaging for extent: Contrast-enhanced CT (or non-contrast CT) of neck and superior mediastinum (defines retrosternal/mediastinal extension, tracheal compression/deviation, and vascular displacement; Thyroid USS is initial exam).

topic: Multinodular Goitre Compressive & Malignancy Red Flags
stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with the longstanding multinodular goitre shown. Which compressive symptom should raise the highest clinical suspicion for invasive thyroid malignancy infiltrating the recurrent laryngeal nerve rather than simple benign mass effect?
options: Mild positional breathlessness when lying flat
Occasional dysphagia to dry solid food boluses
Facial plethora on raising both arms above the head
Progressive new-onset hoarseness of the voice
Visible fullness in the suprasternal notch on swallowing
optionRationales: Incorrect: Positional dyspnoea commonly results from benign tracheal compression by an enlarging goitre.
Incorrect: Mild dysphagia to solids reflects mechanical oesophageal compression by a bulky benign multinodular goitre.
Incorrect: Pemberton's sign (facial plethora/engorged neck veins on arm elevation) reflects benign thoracic inlet crowding from retrosternal extension.

Correct: Progressive hoarseness in a patient with a goitre indicates recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, which strongly raises suspicion for locally invasive thyroid carcinoma rather than benign compression.
Incorrect: Suprasternal fullness moving on swallowing is a standard anatomical sign of a cervical goitre without indicating nerve invasion.
clinicalPearl: Benign multinodular goitres cause stridor/dyspnoea, dysphagia, and Pemberton's sign; new hoarseness means recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion until proven otherwise (perform flexible laryngoscopy).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Pre- and post-operative thyroid assessment requires checking for hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve injury/invasion) alongside stridor and airway compromise.

sourceStation.title: Multinodular Goitre (MNG) — Compressive Symptoms & Imaging
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
1. A 55-year-old woman presented with a multinodular goitre.
1.1 Write two compressive symptoms she could get.
1.2 List two suitable imaging techniques that can be used for investigations.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1.1) Compressive symptoms: Dyspnoea / stridor (tracheal compression), Dysphagia (oesophageal compression), Hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve compression — suspect malignancy), Superior vena cava obstruction / Pemberton's sign (retrosternal extension). (1.2) Imaging techniques: Neck/Thyroid Ultrasound (USS), CT neck and chest (for retrosternal extension/tracheal narrowing), and Chest X-ray (thoracic inlet view).

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with a rapidly enlarging, warm, erythematous breast over 6 weeks showing the pitted skin texture demonstrated in the photographs. What is the pathophysiological cause of the 'peau d'orange' appearance and the most likely diagnosis?
options: Superficial thrombophlebitis of breast veins; Mondor's disease
Acute staphylococcal ductal infection; simple lactational mastitis
Subcutaneous adipocyte saponification; traumatic fat necrosis
Fibrous periductal retraction; benign mammary duct ectasia
Dermal lymphatic tumour emboli; inflammatory breast carcinoma
optionRationales: Incorrect: Mondor's disease produces a tender cord-like superficial vein along the breast/chest wall rather than diffuse orange-peel skin oedema.
Incorrect: Simple mastitis causes erythema and tenderness without persistent woody dermal lymphatic tethering typical of locally advanced carcinoma.
Incorrect: Fat necrosis usually follows trauma or surgery, producing a firm irregular lump rather than diffuse dermal lymphatic engorgement.
Incorrect: Duct ectasia causes subareolar inflammation and slit-like nipple retraction rather than widespread dermal lymphatic oedema.

Correct: Peau d'orange occurs when carcinoma emboli obstruct subdermal lymphatics, producing cutaneous oedema with tethered sweat glands and hair follicles—a hallmark of inflammatory or locally advanced breast carcinoma.
clinicalPearl: Peau d'orange + diffuse erythema without resolution on antibiotics = inflammatory breast carcinoma (T4d); obtain urgent skin punch + core biopsy before neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Locally advanced/inflammatory breast carcinoma presenting with peau d'orange requires urgent tissue biopsy and staging prior to multimodality therapy.

sourceStation.title: Inflammatory Breast Carcinoma / Peau d'Orange
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
5.1 Identify the condition.
5.2 List three features you can see in the pictures.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (5.1) Locally advanced / Inflammatory breast carcinoma. (5.2) Features seen: Peau d'orange (oedema of breast skin with prominent hair follicles due to dermal lymphatic obstruction), Diffuse breast erythema & oedema, Nipple retraction/inversion / asymmetry / ulceration.

domain: 2.3 TRAUMA, SHOCK, BURNS, NEUROTRAUMA & CRITICAL CARE (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 28-year-old motorcyclist is admitted following a head injury. On neurological assessment using the scale shown, he opens his eyes only to painful nail-bed pressure, utters incomprehensible groaning sounds, and exhibits abnormal flexion (decorticate posturing) of the upper limbs to pain. What is his total score and brain injury classification?
options: GCS 6/15 (Moderate brain injury)
GCS 7/15 (Severe brain injury)
GCS 8/15 (Moderate brain injury)
GCS 9/15 (Moderate brain injury)
GCS 10/15 (Severe brain injury)
optionRationales: Incorrect: A score of 6 would correspond to E2 + V1 + M3 or E1 + V2 + M3; eye opening to pain scores 2, incomprehensible sounds 2, and decorticate flexion 3 (sum = 7).
Correct: Eye opening to pain (E2) + incomprehensible sounds (V2) + abnormal flexion/decorticate posturing (M3) totals GCS 7/15, classified as severe brain injury (GCS ≤8).
Incorrect: Not only is the sum 7 rather than 8, but any GCS ≤8 represents severe (not moderate) brain injury.
Incorrect: GCS 9/15 is moderate brain injury (9–12), whereas this patient's components sum to 7.
Incorrect: GCS 10/15 corresponds to moderate brain injury rather than severe, and overestimates this patient's score.
clinicalPearl: Always record individual GCS components (E2 V2 M3 = 7/15): decorticate flexion = M3, decerebrate extension = M2, and total ≤8 defines severe head injury.

guideCitation.keyPoint: GCS sums Eye (1–4), Verbal (1–5), and Motor (1–6); scores ≤8 classify severe head injury (coma), 9–12 moderate, and 13–15 mild.

sourceStation.title: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) Interpretation
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

• What is the score for a fully conscious and ambulant patient?

domain: 2.3 TRAUMA, SHOCK, BURNS, NEUROTRAUMA & CRITICAL CARE (15 STATIONS)
topic: Glasgow Coma Scale Minimum & Maximum Scores
stem: During a surgical trauma round, a house officer evaluates a completely unresponsive patient (no eye opening, no verbal sounds, and no motor response to painful stimuli) alongside a fully conscious, oriented patient using the clinical scoring table shown. What is this scale and its exact minimum and maximum possible scores?
options: AVPU Scale; minimum 0 and maximum 15
Modified Rankin Scale; minimum 0 and maximum 6
Glasgow Coma Scale; minimum 3 and maximum 15
Glasgow Coma Scale; minimum 0 and maximum 15
RASS Sedation Scale; minimum 3 and maximum 18
optionRationales: Incorrect: AVPU is a rapid four-letter categorical trauma screen (Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive) rather than a 3–15 point numerical table.
Incorrect: The Modified Rankin Scale grades post-stroke functional disability from 0 to 6.

Correct: The table represents the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), where each domain (Eye, Verbal, Motor) has a floor of 1—meaning the lowest possible score (even in a clinically deceased patient) is 3 and the maximum is 15.
Incorrect: A common exam pitfall is selecting 0 as the minimum GCS score; because every subscale starts at 1 (E1+V1+M1), the minimum score is 3.
Incorrect: RASS ranges from −5 to +4 for ICU sedation monitoring, not 3 to 18.
clinicalPearl: Classic OSCE viva trap: the lowest possible GCS score—even in a deceased person—is 3 (E1 + V1 + M1), never 0, while normal full consciousness is 15.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Each GCS subscale has a minimum of 1 point, giving a strict range of 3 (deep coma/unresponsive) to 15 (fully conscious and oriented).
